evidence.label: An L² Einstein Gap for Nonnegatively Curved Four-Manifolds

headline: Classifies positive Einstein four-manifolds with nonnegative curvature, and claims a small-energy topological gap.
scope: Closed connected Einstein four-manifolds with positive Einstein constant and sectional curvature ≥ 0. The gap result covers closed simply connected four-manifolds with sectional curvature ≥ 0.
plain: An Einstein space is a curved space whose Ricci curvature, an average of its bending, is the same in every direction. The papers claim that in four dimensions, positive Einstein spaces with no negative bending are only three model shapes, up to covering and scale. A Lean proof covers the case of strictly positive bending. A second paper claims that a space close to Einstein, on average, has the smooth shape of one of the models. That gap result has no Lean check.
doesNot: This does not give a value for the gap constant ε₀, and the gap result says nothing about the metric itself, only the smooth shape. Only the strictly positive classification has a Lean check.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Deane Yang, who listed the three positively curved models as a conjecture
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles a well-known classification question for positively curved Einstein four-manifolds and extends it to the boundary case of zero-curvature planes.

explanation:
Start with two round spheres of radius 1/√3, about 0.577. Each sphere bends by 1/r², which is 3. Now take their product, the four-dimensional space of pairs of points, one on each sphere. A flat piece of a plane inside it can lie along one sphere, or take one direction from each. Along one sphere the bending, called sectional curvature, is 3. Across the two spheres it is 0. Ricci curvature in a direction adds the sectional curvatures of the three planes through it. For a direction along the first sphere this gives 3 + 0 + 0 = 3. Every direction gives 3. A space where Ricci curvature is the same constant in every direction is called Einstein. The round four-sphere of radius 1 is also Einstein: each plane bends by 1, and 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.

Which closed four-dimensional Einstein spaces have no negative bending at all? Closed means finite in size with no edge. In 2000 Yang listed three models for strictly positive bending as a conjecture[1]. They are the round sphere, the round real projective space, and the complex projective plane with its Fubini–Study metric. After scaling to Ricci curvature 3, Fubini–Study bends between 0.5 and 2. Earlier proofs needed extra conditions. Gursky and LeBrun needed a condition on the topology[2]. Cheng needed an Euler characteristic of at most 3[3]. The third paper proves Yang's classification with no such condition[4]. It needs no orientability, so mirror-reversing spaces are included[5].

The main obstacle is in four dimensions only. There the curvature splits into two independent pieces called Weyl blocks. The Einstein equation does not force either block to vanish[6]. The paper shows that one block must vanish, and classical results then name the space. The first paper studies the boundary case, where some plane has zero bending, as in the two-sphere example. An estimate proved for strictly positive bending does not settle that case by itself[7]. It claims that one zero-bending plane forces the universal cover to be the product of two spheres of radius 1/√3[8]. The universal cover is the space unwrapped so that no loop is stuck. Together this gives three models up to covering: the sphere, the complex projective plane, and the product of two spheres[9].

The second paper asks about spaces that are nearly Einstein. It measures the trace-free Ricci energy, the squared gap between Ricci curvature and its average, summed over the space. In four dimensions this number does not change when the space is scaled. For spheres of radii 1 and 2, the product has energy 16π²(2 − 1/2)², about 355.3. Radii 10 and 20 give the same 355.3. The paper claims a universal number ε₀ above zero. A simply connected space with no negative bending and energy below ε₀ has the smooth shape of one of the three models[10]. It needs no bound on volume, diameter or curvature size[11]. The conclusion is about the smooth shape, not the metric[12]. The proof smooths the metric with Ricci flow, an equation that evens out curvature over time[13].

How sure is this? The Lean scope note says the formalization classifies closed Einstein four-manifolds with strictly positive sectional curvature. That covers the third paper's theorem. The zero-plane theorem and the energy gap are not in that note. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds. Lean covers only the strictly positive classification. The zero-plane rigidity and the energy gap have no Lean check, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: How much the space bends along one flat two-dimensional slice through a point.
The sum of the sectional curvatures of the planes through one direction.
A curved space whose Ricci curvature is the same constant in every direction.
The two independent parts of curvature in four dimensions that the Ricci curvature does not fix.
The standard symmetric way to measure distances on the complex projective plane.
The squared difference between Ricci curvature and its average, added up over the whole space.
An equation that changes a metric over time to even out its curvature.
Matched by a smooth map with a smooth inverse; the same smooth shape, perhaps with different distances.
